effects of an assortment of anchor values. We first describe the details of the experiment, and all of
the essential effects present in the data. We then discuss the implementation details of the
between-participants version of AIM and fit it to data. We close the next section by discussing the
modeling results.


4. Experiment 1

   Experiment 1 was intended to test the model across a range of judgment targets and a wide variety
of anchoring effects. The following sections will demonstrate the etiologies of regular anchoring
effects, directional anchors, irrelevant anchors, and the influence of cognitive load on anchoring
effects.


4.1. Methods

    Participants were recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk website (see Buhrmester, Kwang, &
Gosling, 2011; Paolacci, Chandler, & Ipeirotis, 2010, for a review of Mechanical Turk as a viable source
of experimental data) and completed the task in exchange for $0.50. A total of 589 participants (sub
sample information will be provided by condition) completed one of the five between-participant con-
ditions: prior, regular anchors, directional anchors, irrelevant anchors, and cognitive load.
                                  B.M. Turner, D.R. Schley / Cognitive Psychology 90 (2016) 1–47                             13


4.1.1. Materials
    Participants in every condition were presented the same 6 anchoring problems taken from
Simmons et al. (2010) and Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995). The six target questions were as follows:
(1) the length of the Mississippi River, (2) the average annual rainfall in Philadelphia, (3) the maximum
speed of a house cat, (4) the average annual temperature of Phoenix, (5) the population of Chicago, and
(6) the height of the tallest redwood tree. Once the correct answer was determined, for some questions
we set anchors that were either higher or lower than the true value. Questions 1, 3, and 5 used high
anchors (3500 miles, 55 miles per hour, and 5 million people, respectively) whereas Questions 2, 4,
and 6 used low anchors (25 in., 52 °F, and 65 feet, respectively).

4.1.2. Procedure
    The five between-participant conditions are outlined in Table 1. In all conditions participants esti-
mated each of the six target items. Thus, Experiment 1 employed a 5 between-participant (Anchoring
Condition)  6 within-participant (Target Questions) mixed design. In addition to the prior (i.e., unan-
chored control condition) and regular anchor conditions, we included three additional anchoring para-
digms that have received notable attention within the anchoring literature. Because anchors often
provide directional information we included a condition with directional anchors (Simmons et al.,
2010). The literature on irrelevant anchors and numeric primes has been controversial to say the least,
with evidence toward (Adaval & Monroe, 2002; Critcher & Gilovich, 2008; Englich, 2008;
Oppenheimer et al., 2008; Mussweiler & Englich, 2005; Wilson et al., 1996; Wong & Kwong, 2000)
and against (Brewer & Chapman, 2002; Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Frederick & Mochon, 2012;
Mochon & Frederick, 2013; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001) such effects. As such, we included a condition
where the anchors were in reference to items different than those of the target judgments. Lastly,
given the research that used cognitive load as a means of studying anchoring effects (Blankenship,
Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell, & Macy, 2008; Epley & Gilovich, 2001, 2006; van Rooijen &
Daamen, 2006), we included a condition where participants completed the regular anchoring task
under cognitive load. We included this range of conditions to test AIM’s ability to model a range of
anchoring paradigms.
    Borrowing terminology from above, we refer to estimates made by participants in the prior condi-
tion as prior estimates and estimates made by participants in the anchoring conditions as posterior
estimates. Roughly 3% of the data were deleted due to either extremely implausible answers or
because they attempted to look up the answers on-line. We were able to identify the most accessible
answers through Wikipedia, Google, and Yahoo searches. If participants had longer response times
(e.g., greater than 10 s) and answers identical to the ones we identified through these websites, those
observations were deleted. Also as part of the 3% of deletions, estimates in the directional anchoring
condition that were on the incorrect side of the anchor (e.g., an estimate of 4500 miles to an anchor
that was stated to be less than 3500 miles) were deleted. This method of deletions is consistent with
Epley and Gilovich (2001, 2006) and Simmons et al. (2010).

4.2. The model

   To model the data from Experiment 1, we used the between-participant version of AIM described
above. We assumed separate prior representations for each of the six questions, and importantly, this
prior representation was common to all participants. For each question, there were a total of four

Table 1
Outline of between-participant conditions for Experiment 1. The example question that each description below corresponds to is
‘‘What is the length of the Mississippi River?” Key: CL is Cognitive Load.

  Condition                              Description/example
  Prior                                  Unanchored judgment (i.e., no additional information presented)
  Regular                                Is the Mississippi River greater than or less than 3500 miles?
  Directional                            The Mississippi River is less than 3500 miles


5.3.2. The mapping function
    We next define a mapping function to relate the prior consistency variable w to the influence of the
anchor parameter k. In theory, this function may be very complex, requiring many parameters to
relate the two variables precisely for all participants. However, in practice, this function should posit
psychologically meaningful parameters and will likely require some simplifying assumptions to facil-
itate the interpretability of these parameters.
    For simplicity, AIM assumes that as the distance between the prior representation and the anchor
increases, the anchor provides a marginally decreasing influence on the posterior representation, pro-
ducing an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift
from prior to posterior representation. This assumption is informed by the inverted U-shaped relation-
ship observed by Wegener et al. (2001). That said, there are potential special cases where this assump-
tion may not hold. First, if an individual uses an anchor as a hint (Schwarz, 1994; Wegener et al., 2010)
it is feasible to assume that the hint is an exaggeration. If a speaker states that it was ‘‘1,000,000
degrees outside,” the listener may infer that it is ‘‘very hot” outside, as opposed to it actually being
‘‘1,000,000 degrees.” Thus, the anchor would act as a more plausible exemplar (e.g., 125 degrees).
Other anchors (e.g., 500,000 and 1,500,000 degrees) would produce similar effects, resulting in an
asymptoting, rather than inverted-U, relationship between anchor extremity and the size of anchoring
effects (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001). AIM can capture this asymptoting behavior through the param-
eter kmax . Another special case could occur when an individual has no prior information about a target
item. If there is no prior representation, then the posterior representation will be made up entirely of
 24                              B.M. Turner, D.R. Schley / Cognitive Psychology 90 (2016) 1–47


the anchor information. In such a case, the posterior representation will be linearly related to the
anchor.
    For our purposes, we will use the flexible Bézier curve. The Bézier curve uses a set of control points
to influence the path a curve may take. It requires the specification of at least two endpoints that the
curve must pass through, and then any intermediate points can influence the shape of the curve, but
the curve will not pass through these points – except in trivial cases. These requirements turn out to
be helpful in our case, because we can directly build in restrictions on k and w in the specification of
the control points.
    While there are many forms of Bézier curves, we focus on the set of rational Bézier curves that add
adjustable weights to a set of polynomials. The weights in the specification of the Bézier curve will
serve as the parameters in the mapping function. The mapping function will relate the prior consis-
tency variable w (forming the x-axis) to BðwÞ, the proportion of kmax (forming the y-axis), so that
k ¼ BðwÞkmax . Thus, the mapping function is defined on the unit square that ranges from zero to one
on both the x and y axes.
    We begin by specifying both the number n þ 1 and locations P of the control points. As the number
of control points increases, the Bézier curve becomes increasingly more flexible, but the contribution

essential for understanding how consistency might play a role in a participant’s judgment following
the presentation of an anchor. To illustrate this effect, the right panel of Fig. 9 shows the degree of pos-
terior adjustment made as a function of the five values of n in corresponding colors. To calculate the
posterior adjustment, we assumed the prior mean h ¼ 0 (represented as the dashed horizontal and
vertical lines), the prior uncertainty d ¼ 1, and kmax ¼ 2 (for illustrative purposes). Given these inputs
and the level of n, we used Eqs. (4) and (B.11) to determine the mean of the posterior representation
(y-axis) for a range of hypothetical anchor values a (x-axis). Fig. 9 shows an interesting U-shaped pat-
tern that is modulated by the levels of n. Starting near the mean of the prior representation h ¼ 0, we
see little adjustment because the anchor value does not provide information that is unique to the
prior. Hence, the mean of the posterior representation is similar to the mean of the prior representa-
tion. However, as the anchor moves toward the tails of the prior representation, we see that the influ-
ence of the anchor is more pronounced – especially for large values of n – moving the posterior
representation away from the prior representation. However, at some point, the influence of the
anchor declines and AIM reverts back to forming a posterior representation that is more consistent
with the prior representation.


5.4. Summary

    In short, we apply two constraints to extend our within-participant version of AIM First, we assume
that confidence is related to the prior uncertainty parameter. For example, in Experiment 2 we will
assume that across a single continuum H, confidence judgments behave similarly across individuals.

## Study Details

The study titled "The more you ask for, the more you get: Anchoring in personal injury verdicts" was published in Applied Cognitive Psychology in December 1996, volume 10, issue 6, pages 519-540.

## Research Overview

The 'anchoring and adjustment' bias was demonstrated in a personal injury case using mock jurors. In Experiment 1, the ad damnum, or requested compensation, was manipulated across participants. In Experiment 2, anchors were operationalized as the strength of the legal evidence. Both monetary and causal anchors systematically influenced judgments of the probability that the defendant caused the plaintiff's injuries, compensation awarded, and perceptions of the litigants.

## Key Finding

The results indicate that anchoring occurs in legal applications, and that plaintiffs would do well to request large compensation awards.

1. Memory. 2003 Jul-Sep;11(4-5):379-94. doi: 10.1080/09658210244000504.

Hindsight bias as a function of anchor distance and anchor plausibility.

Hardt O(1), Pohl RF.

Author information:
(1)The University of Arizona, Department of Psychology, Tucson 85721, USA. 
[email redacted]

This study explored the influence of anchor distance on hindsight bias and how 
the subjective plausibility of different anchors moderates this relation. In 
addition to the standard memory design used in hindsight bias research, 
participants were asked to indicate the range of values for possible answers to 
difficult almanac questions. Varying anchor distance on the basis of each 
participant's individual range of possible answers showed (1) that anchor 
plausibility decreased with increasing anchor distance following a non-linear 
monotone function, (2) that size of hindsight bias initially increased with 
increasing anchor distance but, from a certain distance, started to decrease, 
and (3) that hindsight bias was found to be always higher for plausible than for 
implausible anchors.

I found relevant information about the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) study on anchoring. Here's what the search results show:

## Study Design

Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) quantified anchoring in numerical estimation using UC Berkeley students (N=156): a calibration group (n=53) first provided estimates and 10-point confidence ratings for 15 uncertain quantities, which defined low/high anchors at the 15th/85th percentiles. An anchored group (n=103) then judged whether each quantity was higher/lower than a provided anchor and gave an estimate plus confidence rating.

## Anchoring Index and Measurement

The Anchoring Index has been described by Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) as the difference between the median estimate in the high and the low anchor condition divided by the distance between the high and low anchor. This procedure permits the transformation of anchored estimates into percentiles in the calibration group, allows pooling of results across problems, and provides a natural measure of the size of the effect.

## Key Findings

Estimates shifted significantly toward anchors across all items. Jacowitz and Kahneman recommend transforming all the estimates in the corresponding percentiles in the calibration group (assigning 0 or 100 to anchor estimates out of the calibration range).

The search results confirm the methodology but don't contain the specific index value of 0.49 or detailed information about asymmetry patterns you mentioned in your query.

Based on the search results, I found information about Mussweiler and Strack's 2000 research on anchoring effects and implausible anchors:

## Key Findings on Implausible Anchors

Whereas plausible anchors activate exemplar knowledge about the target item, implausible anchors activate categorical knowledge.

### Response Time Patterns

Research revealed interesting patterns in how people process different anchor types. Response times during the comparative decision phase are faster for implausible anchors compared to plausible anchors, but response times during the numerical estimate phase are slower for implausible anchors compared to plausible anchors, with this pattern expected if plausible anchors lead to an activation of more elaborate exemplar knowledge during the comparative decision phase, with this more elaborate process occurring during the numerical estimate phase when implausible anchors act as standards.

### Magnitude of Effects

Research on judgmental anchoring has demonstrated that implausible anchors produce large effects. Additionally, implausible anchors that differ extremely produce similar absolute estimates.

### Theoretical Framework

The research supported the Selective Accessibility Model, where an initial phase of hypothesis-consistent testing—retrieving information that supports the anchor's plausibility—is followed by a second phase shaped by that primed knowledge.

10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003 | Anchoring effects on performance judgments | 2008
[no abstract]

10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x | Initiating Salary Discussions With an Extreme Request: Anchoring Effects on Initial Salary Offers1 | 2011
Two studies were conducted to examine the effects of implausible anchors on initial salary offers. Participants provided a salary offer to a candidate after receiving a relevant anchor and an implausible anchor. The results of Study 1 indicated that a high implausible anchor influenced salary offers, even in the presence of the relevant anchor. Study 2 examined whether a more extreme implausible anchor would also affect salary offers. The results indicated that both the high anchor and the extremely high anchor led to higher salary offers than did the control condition.

10.1002/bdm.535 | The long and short of it: physical anchoring effects | 2006
Abstract Attempts to reconstruct the magnitude of recently encountered physical stimuli were influenced by the provision of physical anchors. Whether estimating length, weight, or loudness, those increasing the magnitude of a relatively small (short, light, or quiet) physical anchor produced estimates that were reliably lower than did those decreasing the magnitude of a relatively large (long, heavy, or loud) anchor. Estimates produced without an anchor were also low, suggesting that when people physically adjust upwards from a self‐selected starting point, “no anchor” may, in fact, act as a very low anchor. Physical anchors appear to influence estimates of recently encountered physical stimuli, much as numerical anchors influence estimates of more abstract numerical quantities. Implications for processes underlying anchoring, adjustment, and related tasks are discussed. Copyright © 2006 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5 | The More You Ask For, the More You Get: Anchoring in Personal Injury Verdicts | 1996
The ‘anchoring and adjustment’ bias was demonstrated in a personal injury case using mock jurors. In Experiment 1, the ad damnum, or requested compensation, was manipulated across participants. In Experiment 2, anchors were operationalized as the strength of the legal evidence. Both monetary and causal anchors systematically influenced judgments of the probability that the defendant caused the plaintiff's injuries, compensation awarded, and perceptions of the litigants. These results indicate that anchoring occurs in legal applications, and that plaintiffs would do well to request large compensation awards. In addition, anchors expressed on one scale affected judgments expressed on another scale. This cross-modality anchoring stands in contrast to previous studies. Finally, these anchoring effects are unlikely to be explained by either demand effects or perceived relevance of the anchor.

10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91 | Be careful what you ask for: The effect of anchors on personal-injury damages awards. | 2000
These studies examined the effects of anchors in the context of personal injury damages awards. In 2 experiments, mock jurors read a case in which the presence and size of the plaintiff's damages request and the defense rebuttal were varied across conditions and then awarded damages. Award size and variability increased as the plaintiff's request increased but decreased with the most extreme request. Conversely, award size and variability decreased as the defense rebuttal decreased but increased with the most extreme rebuttal. In both studies, the award recommendations altered the upper and lower boundaries of awards mock jurors found acceptable but did not affect mock jurors' perception of injury severity. The findings suggest that award recommendations can produce biased and unpredictable awards. From Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 2000, Vol. 6, No. 2, 91-103, 2000. DOI: 10.1037//1076-898X.6.2.91 Copyright © 2000 by the American Psychological Association. Reproduced with permission

10.1002/ejsp.52 | The durability of anchoring effects | 2001
Abstract Recent research suggests that judgmental anchoring is mediated by a selective increase in the accessibility of knowledge about the judgmental target. Anchoring thus constitutes one instance of the judgmental effects of increased knowledge accessibility. Such knowledge accessibility effects have repeatedly been demonstrated to be fairly durable, which suggests that the effects of judgmental anchoring may also persist over time. Consistent with this assumption, three experiments demonstrate that judgmental anchors influence judgment even if they were present one week before the critical judgment is made. In fact, the magnitude of anchoring was found to remain undiminished over this period of time. Copyright © 2001 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

"""Implied proportional anchoring indices from published anchor values and mean estimates.

Two-sided AI (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995): (est_high - est_low) / (anchor_high - anchor_low).
One-sided AI: (est - ref) / (anchor - ref), ref = calibration mean inferred from the paper.
Local slope between adjacent anchor levels: d(est) / d(anchor).
Means are used where papers report means; J&K define AI on medians.
"""
from statistics import median


def ai(eh, el, ah, al):
    return (eh - el) / (ah - al)


def show(label, val, note=""):
    print(f"  {label:<48} {val:8.3f}  {note}")


print("Strack & Mussweiler 1997, Study 3 (anchors Table 5 p.442; means Appendix p.446)")
# item: true, plaus_high, plaus_low, impl_high, impl_low, means (pH, pL, iH, iL)
sm97 = {
    "Antarctic winter temp (C)": (-68, -17, -43, 45, -210, -17.1, -36.6, -37.2, -59.8),
    "Einstein first US visit":   (1921, 1939, 1905, 1992, 1215, 1807.3, 1817.4, 1928.2, 1922.1),
    "Da Vinci birth year":       (1452, 1698, 1391, 1952, -300, 1543.6, 1410.3, 1632.9, 1811.1),
    "Gandhi age":                (78, 79, 64, 140, 9, 67.9, 99.6, 66.7, 50.1),
    "Ulm altitude (m)":          (478, 320, 150, 10500, -1700, 276.2, 233.4, 558.1, 490.0),
    "Aristotle birth year":      (-322, -220, -490, 1832, -25000, -297.9, -362.7, -139.5, -1150.4),
    "Whale length (m)":          (33.0, 49.0, 21.0, 900.0, 0.2, 60.1, 29.1, 141.7, 20.5),
    "Elbe length (km)":          (1165, 890, 550, 45000, 25, 676.1, 645.1, 10124.6, 284.7),
}
pl, im = [], []
for k, (t, ph, plo, ih, il, mph, mpl, mih, mil) in sm97.items():
    a_p, a_i = ai(mph, mpl, ph, plo), ai(mih, mil, ih, il)
    pl.append(a_p); im.append(a_i)
    print(f"  {k:<28} plausible AI {a_p:7.3f}   implausible AI {a_i:7.4f}   anchor-gap ratio {(ih-il)/(ph-plo):6.1f}x")
print(f"  median AI plausible {median(pl):.3f}; implausible {median(im):.4f}")
print("  z-score version (Table 6 p.443): plausible diff .17 SD, implausible diff .42 SD")

print("\nMussweiler & Strack 2001 (Table 1 p.154; Table 2 p.156)")
# calibration mean inferred as midpoint of the +-1 SD plausible anchors
for name, anchors, means, ref in [
    ("Study 1 Antarctic (true -68)", (-43, -17, 700, 900), (-41.12, -24.84, -23.27, -24.44), (-43 + -17) / 2),
    ("Study 2 Gandhi (true 78)", (61, 86, 214, 271), (62.92, 70.36, 75.26, 72.86), (61 + 86) / 2),
]:
    a, m = anchors, means
    print(f" {name}; inferred calibration mean {ref}")
    show("two-sided AI plausible pair", ai(m[1], m[0], a[1], a[0]))
    show("two-sided AI implausible pair", ai(m[3], m[2], a[3], a[2]), "(small numerator vs noise)")
    show("AI plausible-low vs implausible-low", ai(m[2], m[0], a[2], a[0]))
    show("AI plausible-low vs implausible-high", ai(m[3], m[0], a[3], a[0]))
    for ak, mk in zip(a, m):
        show(f"one-sided AI anchor {ak}", (mk - ref) / (ak - ref))

print("\nHarris et al. 2019 (Table 2 MS p.23; anchors MS p.17, p.27)")
show("Exp1 UK temp, anchors 8/20", ai(14.70, 12.68, 20, 8))
show("Exp3 UK temp, anchors 2/25", ai(15.88, 10.71, 25, 2))
show("Exp5 UK temp, anchors 2/25", ai(16.16, 11.03, 25, 2))
show("Exp2 car price, anchors 6000/30000", ai(19741.92, 10754.14, 30000, 6000))
show("Exp4 car price, anchors 13000/200000", ai(61452.29, 13817.27, 200000, 13000))

print("\nChapman & Johnson 1994 Exp 1 (Exhibit 3 p.229; values read off figure, +-1)")
# anchors = multiplier x lottery EV; geometric mean EV across the 16 lotteries (Exhibit 2)
evs = [43.69, 128.53, 213.63, 298.47]
gm_ev = 1.0
for e in evs:
    gm_ev *= e
gm_ev **= 0.25
mult = [0.1, 0.7, 1.3, 1.9]
price = [74, 106.5, 127, 127.5]
anc = [x * gm_ev for x in mult]
print(f"  geometric-mean EV {gm_ev:.1f}; anchors {[round(x, 1) for x in anc]}")
for i in range(3):
    show(f"local slope {mult[i]}->{mult[i+1]}", ai(price[i + 1], price[i], anc[i + 1], anc[i]))
show("AI moderate pair 0.7/1.3", ai(price[2], price[1], anc[2], anc[1]))
show("AI extreme pair 0.1/1.9", ai(price[3], price[0], anc[3], anc[0]))

print("\nRusso & Schoemaker 1989 via Lieder et al. Fig. 10 (read off figure; SECONDARY)")
rs_a = [500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300]
rs_m = [630, 680, 790, 885, 990]
rep_m = [590, 645, 870, 970, 1020]
for lab, m in [("R&S 1989", rs_m), ("Lieder MTurk replication", rep_m)]:
    sl = [round(ai(m[i + 1], m[i], rs_a[i + 1], rs_a[i]), 2) for i in range(4)]
    print(f"  {lab}: local slopes {sl}; overall {ai(m[-1], m[0], 1300, 500):.2f}")

print("\nHardt & Pohl 2003 via Wilson et al. Fig. 1 (read off figure; SECONDARY; assumes shift and distance share units)")
d = [0.5, 1, 2, 4, 7]
for lab, hb in [("anchor above estimate", [0.06, 0.11, 0.27, 0.30, 0.22]), ("anchor below estimate", [0.19, 0.25, 0.33, 0.455, 0.40])]:
    print(f"  {lab}: shift/distance {[round(h / x, 3) for h, x in zip(hb, d)]}")

print("\nSchultze et al. 2015 advice-taking curves (Table 1 p.151; pooled p.166-167)")
import math
for lab, b0, b1, b2 in [("Exp1", -0.093, -0.003, 0.153), ("Pooled 6 exps", -0.013, -0.002, 0.101)]:
    vals = {dd: round(b0 + b1 * dd + b2 * math.log(dd), 3) for dd in (5, 20, 40, 64, 75, 150)}
    print(f"  {lab}: weight of advice by distance % {vals}; peak at {-b2 / b1:.1f}%")

The anchoring effect : a meta-analysis
This dissertation proposed and undertook the meta-analysis of the anchoring effect, which utilizes a numeric suggestion to guide subsequent judgments of a target question. Anchoring is thought to operate through a selective accessibility function, such that one who receives an anchor then is primed to access specific information consistent with the number, which in turn pulls a final judgment closer to the anchoring point (Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). This phenomenon is of particular interest in the field of law, where anchors are frequently used to guide sentencing decisions and influence damage awards. Anchoring is frequently cited as a robust and strong effect, but the extent of this potency is unclear. Additionally, a number of moderators (chiefly, expertise and anchor extremity) have been hypothesized, but the true impact of these factors is obscured.Thus, a meta-analysis was conducted, using Schmidt and Hunter's (2014) variance-centric approach. A total of eighty-four effect sizes (Pearson's r) were calculated from the literature, and corrections for artifacts were made where possible. The resulting mean weighted effect size among all included anchoring studies was r = .401, with a corrected correlation estimate of .558. Initial results indicated greater variance than would be expected from sampling error alone, so a number of moderators were evaluated. Expertise was found to be an aggravating moderator; rather than mitigating the effect, having domain-relevant knowledge exacerbated it. Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact. The studies involving a law context (k = 34) were evaluated in a separate analysis, resulting in a mean weighted effect size of r = .360. Additional moderator analyses were conducted, with expertise following a similar pattern as the wider collection of studies. The meaningfulness of the anchor proved to significantly strengthen the effect.The implications of these results were discussed, specifically as they may apply in the courtroom. Future research directions and optimized practices are discussed. The limitations of this meta-analytic approach are acknowledged, and some reflect back upon the optimal practices for this line of research.

Based on the search results, I found information about the study you're looking for. "Be Careful What You Ask For: The Effect of Anchors on Personal Injury Damages Awards" was published in 2000 in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied by Mollie W. Marti and Roselle L. Wissler.

The key findings of this research regarding damage awards and plaintiff requests are: When mock jurors were asked to award $1.5 million, $15 million, or $25 million for pain and suffering, average awards were lowest in the $1.5 million condition, but were higher in the mid-range $15 million condition, because people responded negatively to the $25 million request which was seen as overreaching.

This research demonstrates an important principle about jury damage awards: while larger lump sum requests made by plaintiff's counsel generally result in larger average awards, asking for too much can backfire and lead to rejection of the offer, with moderately high anchors resulting in the most favorable result.

I found the research paper you're looking for! Here's what I found:

"A Rational Account of Anchor Effects in Hindsight Bias" was published in 2021 by Wilson S., Arora S., Zhang Q., and Griffiths T.L. in the Proceedings of the 43rd Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society.

The paper addresses hindsight bias—a cognitive phenomenon where knowledge of an outcome (an anchor) affects subsequent recollections of previous predictions (an estimate). The exact amount of hindsight bias exhibited depends on the anchor value and anchor plausibility, with experimental results showing that hindsight bias is elicited only when the anchor is perceived to be plausible.

The authors present a Bayesian model that captures the relationship between hindsight bias and anchor plausibility, providing a rational account of hindsight bias by considering memory recall as a statistical problem, where the goal is to reconstruct the original estimate using the anchor as new evidence.

jects in the four conditions received the same IO-page packet of informa-

 for each condition. The actual listing price and appraised value for this
 piece of residential real estate was $74,900. The four listing price condi-
 tions were equally distributed around this point: in the “low-price” con-
 dition the property was listed for $65,900; in the “moderately low price”
 condition for $71,900; in the “moderately high price” condition for
 $77,900; and in the “high price” condition for $83,900. These prices were
 used because local real estate agents claimed that any deviation of listing
price from appraisal value of more than 5% would be seen by most real
 estate agents as obviously deviant. The two “moderate” anchors were
4% from the appraisal value; the two extreme anchors were 12% from the
 appraisal value. To facilitate subjects’ decision making, price per square
foot for the property was included on the MLS listing sheet. This piece of
information also differed across groups as a function of the listing price
 differences.
    Amateur subjects. Forty-eight junior and senior undergraduate busi-
 ness school students (30 male, 18 female) participated as subjects. The
 students averaged 22.2 years in age, and had been living in Tucson for an
average of 7.72 years. Of the student subjects, 14.6% had been involved
in a real estate transaction at some time. Each student received extra
credit in an introductory organizational behavior course in exchange for
participation. Prior to participation, subjects were told only that they
would be participating in a study concerned with the pricing of residential
real estate. Subjects were randomly assigned to experimental conditions.
    To prevent contamination across conditions, participants in the same
conditions were transported as a group to the property site. During
transit, subjects reviewed the information packets. No interaction was
allowed between subjects during the transit or while viewing the prop-
erty. Any questions they had were answered individually by the experi-
menter or a research assistant on site at the property. After examining the
property, subjects were transported back to the University; during the
return transport, each subject completed the dependent measure ques-
tionnaire.
    Expert subjects. Twenty-one volunteer real estate agents (17 female, 4
male) from the Tucson area participated as subjects. The average age of
participants was 44.5 years. As a group they had been selling real estate
for 6.99 years, and for 5.77 years in Tucson; they participated in an
average of 12.95 real estate transactions per year. Volunteers were soli-
cited via letters and phone calls to managers of local real estate agencies.
Prior to participation, subjects were told only that they would be partici-

content.text:
## Anchoring vs anchor extremity: per-paper quantitative evidence

I checked every DOI below against `api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>` and the title and first author matched, unless the entry says otherwise. "AI" means the two-sided index: (estimate under high anchor − estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor). "Local slope" is the change in estimate divided by the change in anchor between two adjacent anchor levels. Where a paper gives means rather than the medians Jacowitz & Kahneman specified, I computed the AI on the means.

All arithmetic is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py`. Its output is in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai_out.txt`, and working notes are in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_findings.md`. I opened no data files.

**Source quality at a glance:**
- **Full text read:** Strack & Mussweiler 1997; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Wegener et al. 2001 and 2010; Northcraft & Neale 1987; Bystranowski et al. 2021; Schultze et al. 2015; Turner & Schley 2016; Frederick & Mochon 2012; Smith et al. 2013. Harris et al. 2019, Simmons et al. 2010 and Lieder et al. 2018 are accepted-manuscript or preprint versions, so their page numbers are manuscript pages.
- **Figures only:** Chapman & Johnson 1994. The numbers are read off the figures and are accurate to about ±1.
- **Abstract only:** Townson 2019, Marti & Wissler 2000, Thorsteinson 2011, Lee et al. 2022, Hardt & Pohl 2003.
- **SECONDARY:** Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, Russo & Schoemaker 1989, and the Hardt & Pohl curve. The source is named in each entry.
- **Not obtained:** see the last list in this section.

### 1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, *JBDM* 7:223–242, [10.1002/bdm.3960070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.3960070402) (figures only)
- **How I got it:** I could not download the full text (Wiley paywall; the Chrome download route was off). The Exhibit images come from the author-uploaded copy on academia.edu.
- **Design, Experiment 1:** participants gave selling prices for 16 lotteries. Anchors were 0.1, 0.7, 1.3 and 1.9 × the lottery's expected value (EV), crossed with 4 levels of payoff range (Exhibit 2).
- **Result, Exhibit 3 (p.229):** geometric mean prices were about 74, 106.5, 127 and 127.5.
  - I scaled the anchors by the geometric-mean EV (137.6), giving anchors of 13.8, 96.3, 178.8 and 261.4.
  - Local slopes: 32.5/82.5 = **0.39**, then 20.5/82.5 = **0.25**, then 0.5/82.5 = **0.006**.
  - AI for the moderate pair (0.7/1.3) = **0.25**. AI for the extreme pair (0.1/1.9) = 53.5/247.5 = **0.22**.
  - The curve saturates at the high end only. The low anchor still pulls.
- **Result, Exhibit 4 (p.230), by lottery range.** Extremity here is defined relative to the payoff range:

  | Range | Prices at 0.1 / 0.7 / 1.3 / 1.9 | Shape |
  |---|---|---|
  | Very narrow (extreme anchors far outside the range) | ~84 / 104 / 122 / 111 | inverted-U |
  | Narrow | ~67 / 98 / 104 / 132 | monotone |
  | Wide | ~63 / 106 / 143 / 137 | slight downturn |
  | Very wide | ~83 / 117 / 137 / 123 | downturn |

- **Result, Experiment 2, Exhibit 6 (p.234):** monetary anchors spanned 1.08–28.16 × EV. Prices rose monotonically (about 182, 248, 297, 344). I could not compute an AI because the level multipliers and EVs are in the text I could not read.
- **Abstract (read on the Wiley page):** "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value."
- **Implication:** the AI falls modestly with extremity overall. Raw effects saturate or turn down at the high end, especially when the anchors sit far outside the plausible range.

### 2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997, *JPSP* 73:437–446, [10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437)
- **Design, Study 3:** n=67, 8 items, within-subject. Plausible anchors were about 1 SD from the calibration mean (calibration n=151). Implausible anchors were more than 10 SD away (Table 5, p.442).
- **Result, Table 6 (p.443):** the robust figures are z-scores.
  - Plausible: high .04, low −.13, difference **.17 SD**.
  - Implausible: high .25, low −.17, difference **.42 SD**.
  - Interaction F(1,66)=3.55, p<.07.
- **Implied AI:** a raw shift about 2.5× larger across an anchor gap more than 10× wider means the AI falls to roughly a quarter or less. Caveat: the z-scores are standardised on the study's own responses, not the calibration SD.
- **Appendix (p.446), per-item raw means:** median AI is **0.25** for plausible anchors and **0.06** for implausible ones. Implausible anchor gaps were 7–132× wider.
  - At least the Einstein and Gandhi rows and the Da Vinci implausible pair are internally implausible (e.g., Einstein means around 1807 against anchors of 1905/1939). They are probably typographical errors.
  - Do not rely on the per-item values.
- **Implication:** implausible anchors give a larger raw effect but a much smaller AI.

### 3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705)
This paper has 4 anchor levels per item, and both implausible anchors are high.

- **Study 1, Antarctic mean temperature** (true −68°C; Table 1, p.154; n 15–16 per cell):

  | Anchor | −43 | −17 | 700 | 900 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | −41.12 | −24.84 | −23.27 | −24.44 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~56 SD | ~72 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 16.28/26 = **0.63**.
  - AI implausible pair = −1.17/200 = **−0.006**. The numerator is within noise.
  - AI from the −43 anchor to the 700 anchor = 17.85/743 = **0.024**.
- **Study 2, Gandhi's age at death** (true 78; Table 2, p.156; n 26–28 per cell):

  | Anchor | 61 | 86 | 214 | 271 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Mean estimate | 62.92 | 70.36 | 75.26 | 72.86 |
  | Distance from calibration mean | ~1 SD | ~1 SD | ~18 SD | ~26 SD |

  - AI plausible pair = 7.44/25 = **0.30**.
  - AI implausible pair = **−0.04**.
  - AI from the 61 anchor to the 214 anchor = **0.08**.
- **One-sided AI:** I inferred the calibration mean as the midpoint of the plausible pair (−30°C and 73.5 years).
  - Antarctic: 0.86, 0.40, 0.009, 0.006.
  - Gandhi: 0.85, −0.25, 0.013, −0.003.
  - The inference fails in part for Gandhi. The SD implied by the 61/86 anchors (about 12.5) disagrees with the SD implied by the "18 and 26 SD" statement (about 7.7).
- **Implication:** the raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary. Estimates under implausible anchors are no higher than under the plausible high anchor, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance beyond the boundary.

### 4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001, *JESP* 37:62–69, [10.1006/jesp.2000.1431](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431)
- **Design:** 8 items, each with 6 anchor levels (Appendix, p.68). The design is within-subject 2 (high/low) × 2 (moderate/extreme). Estimates are z-scored per item.
- **Results (pp.65–66):**

  | Study | n | Moderate H/L (difference) | Extreme H/L (difference) | Extreme anchors used |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Exp 1A | 151 | +.50/−.52 (1.02) | +.37/−.36 (0.73) | "Extremely" low/high (e.g., Washington's age 13/167) |
  | Exp 1B | 145 | +.52/−.41 (0.93) | +.15/−.25 (0.40) | "Very extremely" low/high (e.g., 2/167,054) |
  | Exp 2 (no "random anchor" instruction) | 80 | +.40/−.47 (0.87) | +.26/−.19 (0.45) | Same as 1B |

  - Exp 2 plausibility ratings: 1.28 for extreme vs 4.38 for moderate anchors (9-point scale). Rated plausibility mediated the extremity effect for low anchors.
- **Implied AI ratio, extreme vs moderate (illustrative):** I applied the pooled z-difference ratio to each item's anchor gaps.
  - Exp 1A: median ≈ 0.22 (range 0.05–0.26).
  - Exp 1B: median ≈ 0.0015.
- **Implication:** the raw effect is an inverted U, so the AI falls steeply.

### 5. Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010, *J Consumer Psych* 20:5–16, [10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003)
- No new numbers.
- Footnote 1 (p.7) and p.12 cite unpublished raw data (Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty, 2009): with 3 extremity levels, effects were smaller at low and high extremity than at moderate extremity. The downturn came at lower extremity for high-knowledge participants.
- This claim is UNVERIFIED because the data are unpublished.

### 6. Northcraft & Neale 1987, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x) (not in the original list; meets the "≥3 anchor levels" criterion)
- **Design:** listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value (Exp 1, p.88) or ±4% and ±11% (Exp 2, p.92). Realtors described deviations over 5% as "obviously deviant".
- **Exp 1, amateurs, appraisal estimates (Table 1, p.89):** anchors 65.9k, 71.9k, 77.9k, 83.9k gave means 63,571; 67,452; 70,423; 72,196.
  - Local slopes: **0.65, 0.50, 0.30**.
  - AI moderate pair **0.50**; AI extreme pair 8,625/18,000 = **0.48**.
- **Exp 1, experts (Table 2, p.90):** only the two extreme anchors were used. AI = 7,379/18,000 = **0.41**.
- **Exp 2 (Tables 3–4, p.93):** the data are noisy.
  - Experts: AI extreme pair 0.49; AI moderate pair −0.17.
  - Amateurs: AI extreme pair 0.92; AI moderate pair 0.33.
  - Hypothesis 2 (distant anchors have less influence) was not supported.
- **Implication:** within the plausible range (about ±12%), the AI is roughly constant at about 0.5, with mild concavity in Exp 1.

### 7. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, *PSPB* 21:1161–1166, [10.1177/01461672952111004](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) (SECONDARY)
- I could not get the full text (SAGE paywall).
- Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17) reports the empirical mean AI across 15 items as **48.48%**, with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. It also plots the per-item empirical AIs in Fig. 7.
- Lieder's Table C1 gives Lieder's own belief estimates for each item, not J&K's data.
- I could not verify the per-item AIs or the high/low asymmetry.

### 8. Russo & Schoemaker 1989, *Decision Traps* (book, no DOI; SECONDARY via Lieder et al. Fig. 10, manuscript p.21)
- **Design:** one item (year Attila was defeated; true 451). Anchor bins were 500, 700, 900, 1100 and 1300 (each ±100).
- **Result:** means read off the figure were about 630, 680, 790, 885, 990.
  - Local slopes: 0.25, 0.55, 0.47, 0.53. Overall slope **0.45**.
  - The relation is linear, with no saturation up to about 850 years away from the true value.
- **Lieder's MTurk replication:** means of about 590, 645, 870, 970, 1020. The top slope drops to 0.25.

### 9. Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, *PBR* 25:322–349, [10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8) (preprint)
The model predicts two different shapes, depending on which assumption you take.
- **Fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4, p.13):** E[x̂] = a·rᵗ + (1−rᵗ)·x, so the AI is constant across extremity. Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation uses this and predicts a slope of about 0.95. The data show about 0.45.
- **Optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b, p.13).** Distance is measured in σ units of the belief. At a fixed time cost, near anchors are barely adjusted and far anchors are mostly adjusted away. My approximate readings of bias ÷ distance:
  - Time cost ≈ 0.2: about 1.0, 0.85, 0.43, 0.18, 0.03 for anchors 1σ to 5σ away.
  - Time cost ≈ 0.5: about 1.0, 0.98, 0.98, 0.63, 0.26.
- **Implication:** under optimal adjustment the AI falls with extremity measured relative to uncertainty, and the raw bias is non-monotone. This is the prediction to simulate.

### 10. Turner & Schley 2016, *Cognitive Psychology* 90:1–47, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) (PDF from the authors' lab site)
- Section 5.3.2 (pp.23–24) and Fig. 9: the mapping function builds in an inverted-U between anchor extremity and the posterior shift, citing Wegener et al. 2001.
- The model can also produce an asymptote instead, through its maximum-influence parameter.
- Their experiments use one anchor per item, so they give no extremity data.

### 11. Hardt & Pohl 2003, *Memory* 11:379–394, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504) (abstract via PubMed; curve SECONDARY)
- **Design:** hindsight-bias paradigm. Anchor distance was scaled to each participant's own range of plausible answers.
- **Abstract:** plausibility fell with distance; bias first rose, then fell beyond some distance; bias was always higher for plausible anchors.
- **Curve:** Fig. 4 is reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths 2021 (CogSci proceedings; [PDF](https://cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf)), Fig. 1. At distances 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 7, bias ÷ distance was:
  - Anchor above the original estimate: 0.12, 0.11, 0.14, 0.08, 0.03.
  - Anchor below: 0.38, 0.25, 0.17, 0.11, 0.06.
  - This division assumes the two axes share units.
- **Implication:** the raw shift is an inverted U, and the proportional shift falls with distance measured relative to each participant's own uncertainty.

### 12. Bystranowski, Janik, Próchnicki & Skórska 2021, *Law & Human Behavior* 45:1–23, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438)
- **Design:** "anchor value" was coded as a z-score of anchor magnitude between studies, binned at the 25th and 75th percentiles. It is not extremity relative to the true value or to uncertainty.
- **Control vs anchor designs (Table 4, p.12):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 4 | .43 |
  | Medium | 42 | .59 |
  | High | 5 | .19 |

  - As a continuous moderator: coefficient −.04 (z′) and −.08 (d), not significant.
- **High vs low designs (Table 5, p.13):**

  | Anchor value | k | d |
  |---|---|---|
  | Low | 5 | .82 |
  | Medium | 25 | 1.00 |
  | High | 7 | .77 |

  - The text states the continuous slope was negative in both design types.
- **Authors' summary (p.17):** moderate anchors produced the largest effects, but not significantly so.

### 13. Townson 2019, PhD dissertation, Michigan State University, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite; abstract only)
- Meta-analysis of 84 effect sizes (r), mean r = .401.
- Abstract: "Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact." The size and coding of that effect are not in the abstract, and I could not get past the repository's bot check.

### 14. Harris et al. 2019, *JEP:General* 148:e30–e50, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644) (accepted manuscript)
- **Design:** the same two items were tested with different anchor gaps across experiments. Means are in Table 2 (p.23).
- **UK average temperature:**
  - Anchors 8/20°C (p.17): AI = 2.02/12 = **0.17**.
  - Anchors 2/25°C (p.27): AI = **0.225** in Exp 3 and **0.22** in Exp 5.
- **UK new-car price:**
  - Anchors £6,000/£30,000: AI = **0.37**.
  - Anchors £13,000/£200,000: AI = **0.255**.
- **Inconsistency in the manuscript:** the discussion on p.26 describes the Exp 1–2 anchors as 10/18°C and £20,000. With 10/18°C the temperature AI is **0.25**.
- **Implication:** the two items move in opposite directions as the anchor gap widens.

### 15. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010, *JPSP* 99:917–932, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540) (Penn repository manuscript)
- Single-anchor design with plausible vs implausible anchors (Tables 2–3, manuscript pp.47–48). An AI cannot be computed.
- Note 2 (p.42): implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items.
- The main finding: accuracy incentives increased adjustment only away from implausible anchors.

### 16. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015, *JDM* 10:144–171, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922) (advice-taking analogue)
- Exp 1 (Table 1, p.151): weight of advice = −0.093 − 0.003·d + 0.153·ln d, with d as percent distance. This gives about 0.14 at 5%, 0.35 at 40–64%, and 0.34 at 75%. The peak at about 51% is my calculation from the rounded coefficients.
- Pooled across 6 experiments (pp.166–167): B1 = −0.002, B2 = 0.101. The paper states the peak is at **63.84%**. The downturn at far distances is shallow.
- Absolute opinion shift rose roughly in proportion to distance, with no downturn up to 150%.
- **Implication:** the proportional index is an inverted U, driven mainly by advice near one's own estimate being ignored. The linear-plus-log form is a ready template for the AI-vs-distance curve.

### 17. Marti & Wissler 2000, *JEP:Applied* 6:91–103, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91) (abstract only)
- Abstract: awards rose with the plaintiff's request "but decreased with the most extreme request."
- Request levels are SECONDARY (plaintiffmagazine.com): $1.5M, $15M and $25M.
- **Conflict:** Bystranowski et al. (p.6) cite this paper and Chapman & Bornstein 1996 as showing awards rising "even when the anchor is outlandishly high". That contradicts this abstract.

### 18. Other entries
- **Thorsteinson 2011**, *JASP* 41:1774–1792, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x) (abstract only): both the high implausible anchor and the extremely high one raised salary offers above control. The abstract gives no comparison between them.
- **Lee, Lee & Kim 2022**, *Korean J Cognitive Science* 33(1):77–93, 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004: the DOI resolves to the KCI portal but is not in Crossref. From the abstract only: extreme anchors produced smaller anchoring than plausible ones, and difficult items produced larger anchoring.
- **Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013**, *EJSP* 43:97–108, [10.1002/ejsp.1921](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.1921): Fig. 3 (p.105) only hypothesises a plateau that comes earlier for high-knowledge people. Not tested.
- **Frederick & Mochon 2012**, *JEP:General* 141:124–133, [10.1037/a0024006](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024006): no extremity manipulation.
- **Quattrone et al. 1984:** unpublished; claims an asymptote. UNVERIFIED; cited by Wegener et al. 2001, p.63.
- **Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte & Vadillo 2020**, *Collabra* [10.1525/collabra.310](https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.310): about incidental anchors, not extremity.

**Not obtained (paywalled, no open copy found):**
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2000**, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
- **Thorsteinson et al. 2008**, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
- **LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006**, [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535). Note the brief listed 10.1002/bdm.536, which is a different paper. The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Mussweiler 2001**, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52). The abstract does not mention extremity.
- **Chapman & Bornstein 1996**, [10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5](https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5). The download tool returned an unrelated law-review article, which I discarded.

## Synthesis

**Existing quantitative predictions and findings:**
- **Within the plausible range, estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor, so the AI is roughly flat.**
  - Russo & Schoemaker: slope ≈ 0.45.
  - Jacowitz & Kahneman: mean AI ≈ 0.48.
  - Northcraft & Neale: 0.48–0.50.
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2001 plausible pairs: 0.30–0.63.
  - Chapman & Johnson moderate pair: 0.25.
  - Harris: 0.17–0.37.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.**
  - Plateau: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; the high end of Chapman & Johnson.
  - Decline: Wegener 1A/1B/2; the Marti & Wissler abstract; the high bin in Bystranowski; Townson; the Hardt & Pohl curve.
- **Counter-evidence and caveats:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997 found a larger raw effect for implausible anchors, though the implied AI is still smaller.
  - Simmons note 2 found larger anchoring from implausible anchors on 6 of 8 items.
  - The Harris temperature item's AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2 kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 3 shows a high/low asymmetry: saturation at the high end, not the low end.
- **Theoretical curves already stated in the literature:**
  - Linear, diminishing, or "contrast" (inverted-U): Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 1, p.225.
  - Inverted-U by assumption: Turner & Schley.
  - Asymptote: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Quattrone et al.
  - Constant AI (fixed adjustments) versus falling AI (optimal adjustments): Lieder et al.

**Gaps the planned study would fill:**
- No study reports the proportional AI across three or more extremity levels that span both sides of the plausibility boundary, with per-item means and a calibration SD, on more than two items.
  - The nearest are Chapman & Johnson (lotteries; figures only), Mussweiler & Strack 2001 (two items; implausible anchors all high), Northcraft & Neale (one house per experiment; ±12% only) and Russo & Schoemaker (one item; secondary).
- Only Hardt & Pohl scale distance to each person's own uncertainty, and that is hindsight bias with secondary numbers.
- No study fits the competing models (resource-rational adjustment, anchor integration, insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility) to item-level AI-versus-extremity curves.
- The existing meta-analyses (Bystranowski, Townson) code extremity as raw anchor magnitude or as a crude category, not relative to truth or uncertainty.

content.text:
## Anchoring vs anchor extremity: findings (wrap-up)

The per-paper report is complete. The full version, with page references for every number, is in my previous message. The files are:
- `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_findings.md` (notes per paper)
- `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py` (all AI arithmetic; rerunnable)
- `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai_out.txt` (its output)

I opened no data files.

AI below means (estimate under high anchor − estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor), computed on means unless stated. Every DOI was checked against Crossref, except the Townson and Lee et al. DOIs, which are noted where they appear.

**Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995**, *PSPB* 21:1161–1166, [10.1177/01461672952111004](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004):
- I could not get the full text (SAGE paywall). The only number I have is SECONDARY: a mean empirical AI of **48.48% across 15 items**, with anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles. This comes from Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17).
- The per-item AIs and the high/low asymmetry are UNVERIFIED.
- Lieder's Table C1 lists Lieder's own belief estimates for each J&K item, not J&K's data.

### Per paper

- **Chapman & Johnson 1994**, *JBDM* 7:223–242, [10.1002/bdm.3960070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.3960070402). Figures only, read off to about ±1; the text is UNVERIFIED.
  - Experiment 1 (Exhibit 3, p.229): anchors of 0.1, 0.7, 1.3 and 1.9 × the lottery's expected value gave prices of about 74, 106.5, 127 and 127.5.
  - Local slopes were 0.39, 0.25 and 0.006. The AI was 0.25 for the moderate pair and 0.22 for the extreme pair.
  - The curve saturates at the high end only.
  - Exhibit 4 (p.230): when the extreme anchors fall far outside the lottery's payoff range, the curve is an inverted U (about 84, 104, 122, 111).
- **Strack & Mussweiler 1997**, *JPSP* 73:437–446, [10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437).
  - Table 6 (p.443), in z-scores: the high−low difference was 0.17 SD for plausible anchors (about 1 SD from the calibration mean) and 0.42 SD for implausible anchors (more than 10 SD away).
  - So the raw effect was about 2.5× larger across an anchor gap more than 10× wider, which means a much smaller AI.
  - The per-item Appendix (p.446) gives median AIs of 0.25 vs 0.06, but several rows look like typographical errors. Do not rely on them.
- **Mussweiler & Strack 2001**, *Social Cognition* 19:145–160, [10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705).
  - Antarctic temperature: anchors −43, −17, 700, 900 gave means −41.1, −24.8, −23.3, −24.4. The AI was 0.63 for the plausible pair and −0.006 for the implausible pair.
  - Gandhi's age: anchors 61, 86, 214, 271 gave means 62.9, 70.4, 75.3, 72.9. The AI was 0.30 for the plausible pair and −0.04 for the implausible pair.
  - The raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance beyond it.
- **Wegener et al. 2001**, *JESP* 37:62–69, [10.1006/jesp.2000.1431](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431).
  - The z-scored high−low difference was about 1.0 for moderate anchors in every study. For the more extreme anchors it was 0.73 (Exp 1A), 0.40 (Exp 1B) and 0.45 (Exp 2) (pp.65–66).
  - The raw effect is an inverted U. The implied AI for extreme vs moderate anchors is about 0.22 of the moderate value in 1A and about 0.0015 in 1B. These ratios are illustrative only.
- **Wegener et al. 2010**, [10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003): no numbers of its own. It cites unpublished 3-level data showing an inverted U whose downturn comes earlier for high-knowledge people (UNVERIFIED).
- **Northcraft & Neale 1987**, *OBHDP* 39:84–97, [10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x).
  - Four listing-price anchors at ±4% and ±12% of the true value.
  - Experiment 1, amateurs: local slopes 0.65, 0.50, 0.30; AI 0.50 for the moderate pair and 0.48 for the extreme pair.
  - Experts: AI 0.41. Experiment 2 data are noisy.
- **Russo & Schoemaker 1989** (SECONDARY; read off Lieder et al.'s Fig. 10): anchors 500–1300 for the year Attila was defeated (true 451) gave means of about 630 to 990. The slope is about 0.45 and linear.
- **Lieder et al. 2018**, [10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8).
  - With a fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4), the AI is constant across extremity.
  - With the optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b), the AI falls with distance measured in units of uncertainty. These are approximate figure readings.
  - Their Russo & Schoemaker simulation predicts a slope of about 0.95 against the observed 0.45.
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003): the model assumes an inverted U by construction (pp.23–24) and can also produce an asymptote. It has no extremity data.
- **Hardt & Pohl 2003**, [10.1080/09658210244000504](https://doi.org/10.1080/09658210244000504): hindsight-bias paradigm, with distance scaled to each person's own range of plausible values.
  - The raw shift is an inverted U. The shift divided by distance falls from about 0.12–0.38 to 0.03–0.06.
  - Abstract seen; curve SECONDARY via Wilson et al. 2021, CogSci proceedings.
- **Bystranowski et al. 2021**, [10.1037/lhb0000438](https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000438): uses between-study anchor magnitude, not extremity relative to the truth.
  - Control-vs-anchor designs (Table 4, p.12): d = .43, .59, .19 for low, medium and high anchor values.
  - High-vs-low designs (Table 5, p.13): d = .82, 1.00, .77.
  - The continuous slopes were negative but not significant.
- **Townson 2019**, dissertation, [10.25335/p9dm-7a29](https://doi.org/10.25335/p9dm-7a29) (verified via DataCite, not Crossref). Abstract only: extremity "slightly weaken[s]" the effect. The size of that effect is UNVERIFIED.
- **Harris et al. 2019**, [10.1037/xge0000644](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000644).
  - Temperature AI rose from 0.17 to 0.22 when the anchor gap widened. It is 0.25 instead of 0.17 under the manuscript's other description of the Exp 1 anchors.
  - Car-price AI fell from 0.37 to 0.26.
- **Simmons et al. 2010**, [10.1037/a0021540](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021540): a single anchor per item, so no AI. Implausible anchors left estimates further from the truth on 6 of 8 items (note 2).
- **Schultze et al. 2015**, [10.1017/s1930297500003922](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922): an advice-taking analogue. The weight given to advice is an inverted U, modelled as a linear term plus a log term, peaking at 63.84% advice distance. The absolute shift keeps rising with distance.
- **Abstract only:**
  - Marti & Wissler 2000, [10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91](https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91): awards fell at the most extreme request. Bystranowski et al. cite this paper as showing no decline.
  - Thorsteinson 2011, [10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x).
  - Lee et al. 2022 (10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004; resolves via doi.org but is not in Crossref): extreme anchors produced smaller effects than plausible ones.
- **Not obtained (UNVERIFIED):**
  - Mussweiler & Strack 2000, [10.1006/jesp.1999.1414](https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1999.1414).
  - Thorsteinson et al. 2008, [10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003).
  - LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006: the correct DOI is [10.1002/bdm.535](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.535), not bdm.536.
  - Mussweiler 2001, [10.1002/ejsp.52](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.52).
  - Chapman & Bornstein 1996: the download tool returned the wrong paper, which I discarded.

### Synthesis

- **Within the plausible range, the AI is roughly flat at about 0.25–0.6.** Estimates rise roughly linearly with the anchor.
- **At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus or declines, so the AI falls roughly as 1/distance.** The Lieder model with optimal adjustment predicts the same falling AI.
- **Counter-cases:**
  - Strack & Mussweiler 1997: the raw effect was larger for implausible anchors.
  - Chapman & Johnson Experiment 2: estimates kept rising across a 26-fold anchor range.
  - Harris temperature item: the AI rose as the anchor gap widened.
  - High/low asymmetry: Chapman & Johnson saturate at the high end only.
- **Gap:** no study reports the AI at three or more levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items, with item-level means and a calibration SD. No study fits the four candidate models to item-level curves. The existing meta-analyses code extremity as raw anchor magnitude, not relative to the truth or to uncertainty.

input.content:
# Anchoring vs anchor extremity: quantitative evidence from primary texts

AI = (est_high − est_low) / (anchor_high − anchor_low) (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995), computed on means unless stated.
"Local slope" = change in estimate / change in anchor between adjacent anchor levels.
All arithmetic: `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py` (output `_ai_out.txt`). Notes: `_findings.md`.
DOIs verified via api.crossref.org (title + first author match) unless marked otherwise. No data files opened.

Provenance tags: FULL = full text read; FIG = figures only; ABS = abstract only; SECONDARY = numbers from another source (named); UNVERIFIED = not checked against the primary source.

## 1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, JBDM 7:223–242, doi 10.1002/bdm.3960070402 — FIG
- Full text not obtained (Wiley paywall). Exhibit images from the author's academia.edu upload; values read off figures (±1). Abstract (Wiley page): "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value".
- Exp 1: selling prices for 16 lotteries (4 EVs × 4 payoff ranges; Exhibit 2). Anchors = 0.1, 0.7, 1.3, 1.9 × EV.
- Exhibit 3 (p.229): geometric-mean prices ≈ 74, 106.5, 127, 127.5. Anchors scaled by geometric-mean EV 137.6 → 13.8, 96.3, 178.8, 261.4.
  - Local slopes: 32.5/82.5 = 0.39; 20.5/82.5 = 0.25; 0.5/82.5 = 0.006.
  - AI moderate pair (0.7/1.3) = 0.25; AI extreme pair (0.1/1.9) = 53.5/247.5 = 0.22.
  - Saturation at the high end only (high/low asymmetry).
- Exhibit 4 (p.230), by payoff range (extremity relative to plausible range):
  - very narrow (extreme anchors far outside range): ≈ 84 / 104 / 122 / 111 → inverted U
  - narrow: ≈ 67 / 98 / 104 / 132 → monotone
  - wide: ≈ 63 / 106 / 143 / 137; very wide: ≈ 83 / 117 / 137 / 123 → downturn at 1.9
- Exp 2, Exhibit 6 (p.234): monetary anchors 1.08–28.16 × EV → prices ≈ 182 / 248 / 297 / 344, monotone. AI not computable (multipliers per level in unread text; UNVERIFIED).
- Implication: AI falls modestly with extremity; raw effect saturates or turns down when anchors lie far outside the plausible range.

## 2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997, JPSP 73:437–446, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437 — FULL
- Study 3: n = 67, 8 items, within-subject 2 (high/low) × 2 (plausible/implausible). Plausible anchors ≈ 1 SD from the calibration mean (n = 151); implausible > 10 SD (Table 5, p.442).
- Table 6 (p.443), z-scored estimates: plausible high .04 / low −.13 (diff .17 SD); implausible high .25 / low −.17 (diff .42 SD). Interaction F(1,66) = 3.55, p < .07.
- Implied: raw shift ≈ 2.5× larger over an anchor gap > 10× wider → AI ≈ ¼ or less. Caveat: z standardised on the study's own responses, not calibration SD.
- Appendix (p.446) per-item raw means: median AI plausible 0.25, implausible 0.06 (implausible anchor gaps 7–132× wider). Einstein, Gandhi and Da Vinci-implausible rows are internally implausible (e.g., Einstein means ≈ 1807 with anchors 1905/1939); likely typographical. Do not rely on per-item values.
- Implication: larger raw effect but much smaller AI for implausible anchors.

## 3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001, Social Cognition 19:145–160, doi 10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705 — FULL
- 4 anchor levels per item; both implausible anchors high.
- Study 1, Antarctic mean temp (true −68 °C; Table 1, p.154; n 15–16/cell): anchors −43, −17 (±1 SD), 700, 900 (≈ 56 and 72 SD) → means −41.12, −24.84, −23.27, −24.44.
  - AI plausible = 16.28/26 = 0.63; AI implausible = −1.17/200 = −0.006 (within noise); AI −43→700 = 17.85/743 = 0.024.
- Study 2, Gandhi age (true 78; Table 2, p.156; n 26–28/cell): anchors 61, 86 (±1 SD), 214, 271 (≈ 18, 26 SD) → means 62.92, 70.36, 75.26, 72.86.
  - AI plausible = 7.44/25 = 0.30; AI implausible = −0.04; AI 61→214 = 0.08.
- One-sided AI with calibration mean inferred as midpoint of plausible pair (−30 °C; 73.5 yrs): Antarctic 0.86, 0.40, 0.009, 0.006; Gandhi 0.85, −0.25, 0.013, −0.003. Inference is shaky for Gandhi (SD implied by 61/86 ≈ 12.5 vs by "18 and 26 SD" ≈ 7.7).
- Implication: raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary → AI ≈ 1/distance beyond it.

## 4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001, JESP 37:62–69, doi 10.1006/jesp.2000.1431 — FULL
- 8 items, 6 anchor levels each (Appendix, p.68); within-subject 2 × 2 (high/low × moderate/extreme); z-scored estimates.
- Exp 1A (n = 151): moderate +.50/−.52 (diff 1.02) vs extreme (e.g., Washington age 13/167) +.37/−.36 (0.73).
- Exp 1B (n = 145): moderate +.52/−.41 (0.93) vs very extreme (e.g., 2/167,054) +.15/−.25 (0.40).
- Exp 2 (n = 80, no "random anchor" instruction): moderate +.40/−.47 (0.87) vs very extreme +.26/−.19 (0.45). Plausibility 1.28 vs 4.38 (9-pt); rated plausibility mediated the extremity effect for low anchors (pp.65–66).
- Implied AI ratio extreme/moderate (illustrative: pooled z-diff ratio ÷ per-item anchor-gap ratio): 1A median ≈ 0.22 (0.05–0.26); 1B median ≈ 0.0015.
- Implication: raw effect inverted U; AI falls steeply.

## 5. Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010, J Consumer Psych 20:5–16, doi 10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003 — FULL
- No new numbers. Footnote 1 (p.7), p.12 cite unpublished raw data (Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty 2009): 3 extremity levels, smaller effects at low and high than moderate extremity; downturn earlier for high-knowledge people. UNVERIFIED (unpublished).

## 6. Northcraft & Neale 1987, OBHDP 39:84–97, doi 10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x — FULL
- Listing-price anchors ±4% and ±12% of true value (Exp 1, p.88) or ±4%/±11% (Exp 2, p.92). Realtors said > 5% deviation is "obviously deviant".
- Exp 1 amateurs, appraisal (Table 1, p.89): anchors 65.9k / 71.9k / 77.9k / 83.9k → 63,571 / 67,452 / 70,423 / 72,196. Local slopes 0.65, 0.50, 0.30; AI moderate 0.50; AI extreme 8,625/18,000 = 0.48.
- Exp 1 experts, extreme anchors only (Table 2, p.90): AI = 7,379/18,000 = 0.41.
- Exp 2 (Tables 3–4, p.93), noisy: experts AI extreme 0.49, moderate −0.17; amateurs AI extreme 0.92, moderate 0.33. H2 (distant anchors less influential) not supported.
- Implication: within the plausible range (±12%), AI ≈ 0.5, roughly constant, mild concavity in Exp 1.

## 7. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, PSPB 21:1161–1166, doi 10.1177/01461672952111004 — SECONDARY
- Full text not obtained (SAGE paywall).
- Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17): empirical mean AI = 48.48% over 15 items; anchors at 15th/85th percentiles of calibration group. Lieder Fig. 7 plots per-item empirical AI.
- Per-item AIs and high/low asymmetry UNVERIFIED. Lieder Table C1 lists Lieder's own belief estimates (µ, σ) for J&K items, not J&K data.

## 8. Russo & Schoemaker 1989, Decision Traps (book, no DOI) — SECONDARY via Lieder et al. Fig. 10 (manuscript p.21)
- One item: year Attila defeated (true 451); anchor bins 500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300 (±100).
- Means read off figure ≈ 630, 680, 790, 885, 990 → local slopes 0.25, 0.55, 0.47, 0.53; overall 0.45; linear, no saturation ~850 years from truth.
- Lieder MTurk replication ≈ 590, 645, 870, 970, 1020 → top slope 0.25.

## 9. Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, PBR 25:322–349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 — FULL (preprint)
- Fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4, p.13): E[x̂] = a·rᵗ + (1−rᵗ)·x → constant AI across extremity. R&S simulation with J&K-fitted parameters predicts slope ≈ 0.95 vs observed ≈ 0.45.
- Optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b, p.13; distance in σ units): near anchors barely adjusted, far anchors mostly adjusted away. Approx. bias/distance (figure readings): time cost ≈ 0.2 → 1.0, 0.85, 0.43, 0.18, 0.03 for 1σ–5σ; time cost ≈ 0.5 → 1.0, 0.98, 0.98, 0.63, 0.26.
- Implication: under optimal adjustment AI falls with extremity relative to uncertainty; raw bias non-monotone.

## 10. Turner & Schley 2016, Cognitive Psychology 90:1–47, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003 — FULL (lab-site PDF)
- Sec. 5.3.2 (pp.23–24), Fig. 9: mapping function builds in an inverted U between anchor extremity and posterior shift (citing Wegener 2001); parameter kmax allows an asymptote instead. Experiments use one anchor per item: no extremity data.

## 11. Hardt & Pohl 2003, Memory 11:379–394, doi 10.1080/09658210244000504 — ABS + SECONDARY
- Hindsight paradigm; anchor distance scaled to each participant's own range of plausible values.
- Abstract (PubMed 14562869): plausibility fell with distance; bias rose then fell; bias always higher for plausible anchors.
- Fig. 4 reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths 2021 (Proc. 43rd CogSci; cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf), Fig. 1. Bias/distance at distances 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 7: anchor above estimate 0.12, 0.11, 0.14, 0.08, 0.03; below 0.38, 0.25, 0.17, 0.11, 0.06 (assumes shared units).
- Implication: raw shift inverted U; proportional shift falls with distance relative to own uncertainty.

## 12. Bystranowski, Janik, Próchnicki & Skórska 2021, Law & Human Behavior 45:1–23, doi 10.1037/lhb0000438 — FULL
- "Anchor value" = between-study z-score of anchor magnitude, binned at 25th/75th percentiles; not extremity relative to truth or uncertainty.
- Table 4 (p.12), control vs anchor: low k = 4 d = .43; medium k = 42 d = .59; high k = 5 d = .19; continuous coef −.04 (z′), −.08 (d), n.s.
- Table 5 (p.13), high vs low: low k = 5 d = .82; medium k = 25 d = 1.00; high k = 7 d = .77; continuous slope negative (text), n.s.
- p.17: moderate anchors largest effects, not significant.

## 13. Townson 2019, PhD dissertation, Michigan State Univ., doi 10.25335/p9dm-7a29 (DataCite verified) — ABS
- Meta-analysis, k = 84 r effect sizes, mean r = .401. "Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact." Size and coding UNVERIFIED (repository bot check blocked full text).

## 14. Harris et al. 2019, JEP:General 148:e30–e50, doi 10.1037/xge0000644 — FULL (accepted MS)
- Same items with different anchor gaps across experiments; means Table 2 (p.23).
- UK temperature: anchors 8/20 °C (p.17) → AI 2.02/12 = 0.17; anchors 2/25 °C (p.27) → 0.225 (Exp 3), 0.22 (Exp 5).
- UK car price: £6,000/£30,000 → 0.37; £13,000/£200,000 → 0.255.
- Internal inconsistency: p.26 describes Exp 1–2 anchors as 10/18 °C and £20,000; with 10/18 °C, temperature AI = 0.25.
- Implication: the two items move in opposite directions as the anchor gap widens.

## 15. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010, JPSP 99:917–932, doi 10.1037/a0021540 — FULL (Penn repository MS)
- Single anchor per item, plausible vs implausible (Tables 2–3, MS pp.47–48); no AI computable.
- Note 2 (MS p.42): implausible anchors left estimates further from truth on 6/8 items. Main finding: incentives increased adjustment only away from implausible anchors.

## 16. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015, JDM 10:144–171, doi 10.1017/s1930297500003922 — FULL (advice-taking analogue)
- Exp 1 (Table 1, p.151): weight of advice = −0.093 − 0.003·d + 0.153·ln d (d = % distance) → ≈ 0.14 at 5%, 0.35 at 40–64%, 0.34 at 75%; peak ≈ 51% (my calculation from rounded coefficients).
- Pooled 6 experiments (pp.166–167): B1 = −0.002, B2 = 0.101; paper states peak at 63.84%; shallow far-distance downturn.
- Absolute opinion shift ≈ proportional to distance, no downturn up to 150%.
- Implication: proportional index inverted U, driven mainly by ignoring near advice; linear-plus-log form is a template for AI-vs-distance.

## 17. Marti & Wissler 2000, JEP:Applied 6:91–103, doi 10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91 — ABS
- Abstract: awards rose with plaintiff request "but decreased with the most extreme request". Request levels $1.5M, $15M, $25M are SECONDARY (plaintiffmagazine.com).
- Conflict: Bystranowski et al. (p.6) cite this paper and Chapman & Bornstein 1996 as showing awards rising "even when the anchor is outlandishly high".

## 18. Other
- Thorsteinson 2011, JASP 41:1774–1792, doi 10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x — ABS: both high implausible and extremely high anchors raised salary offers vs control; no comparison between them in the abstract.
- Lee, Lee & Kim 2022, Korean J Cognitive Science 33(1):77–93, doi 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004 (resolves via doi.org to KCI; not in Crossref) — ABS: extreme anchors smaller effects than plausible; difficult items larger effects.
- Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013, EJSP 43:97–108, doi 10.1002/ejsp.1921 — FULL: Fig. 3 (p.105) hypothesises a plateau reached earlier by high-knowledge people; not tested.
- Frederick & Mochon 2012, JEP:General 141:124–133, doi 10.1037/a0024006 — FULL: no extremity manipulation.
- Quattrone et al. 1984, unpublished (asymptote claim) — UNVERIFIED; cited in Wegener et al. 2001, p.63.
- Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte & Vadillo 2020, Collabra, doi 10.1525/collabra.310: incidental anchors, not extremity.

## Not obtained (UNVERIFIED)
- Mussweiler & Strack 2000, doi 10.1006/jesp.1999.1414
- Thorsteinson et al. 2008, doi 10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003
- LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006, doi 10.1002/bdm.535 (the brief's 10.1002/bdm.536 is a different paper); abstract does not mention extremity
- Mussweiler 2001, doi 10.1002/ejsp.52; abstract does not mention extremity
- Chapman & Bornstein 1996, doi 10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5 (download tool returned a wrong paper; discarded)

## Synthesis

What the literature shows:
- Within the plausible range, AI is roughly flat: R&S slope ≈ 0.45; J&K mean AI ≈ 0.48; Northcraft & Neale 0.48–0.50; M&S 2001 plausible pairs 0.30–0.63; C&J moderate pair 0.25; Harris 0.17–0.37.
- At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus (M&S 2001; C&J high end) or declines (Wegener 1A/1B/2; Marti & Wissler abstract; Bystranowski high bin; Townson; Hardt & Pohl), so AI falls roughly as 1/distance.
- Counter-cases: S&M 1997 raw effect larger for implausible anchors (AI still smaller); Simmons note 2; C&J Exp 2 monotone rise over 1.08–28.16 × EV; Harris temperature AI rose with wider gap; C&J Exhibit 3 high/low asymmetry.

Stated theoretical curves:
- Linear / diminishing / contrast (inverted U): Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 1, p.225.
- Inverted U by assumption: Turner & Schley 2016.
- Asymptote: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Quattrone et al. 1984.
- Constant AI (fixed adjustments) vs falling AI (optimal adjustments): Lieder et al. 2018.

Gaps the planned study fills:
- No study reports proportional AI across ≥ 3 levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items with item-level means and a calibration SD. Nearest: C&J 1994 (lotteries; figures only), M&S 2001 (2 items; all-high implausibles), Northcraft & Neale (1 house per experiment; ±12% only), R&S (1 item; secondary).
- Only Hardt & Pohl scale distance to each person's own uncertainty (hindsight paradigm; secondary numbers).
- No study fits the competing models (resource-rational, anchor integration, insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility) to item-level AI-vs-extremity curves.
- Meta-analyses (Bystranowski, Townson) code extremity as raw magnitude or a crude category, not relative to truth or uncertainty.
